faq.q: Why does my brain keep saying what if?
faq.a: Your brain is trying to protect you by guessing problems before they happen. But it often guesses the worst, so the what-ifs feel much scarier than real life.
asks: Why do I keep thinking bad things will happen?

faq.q: Why can worry stop me sleeping?
faq.a: Worry switches on your brain's alarm, and an alarm makes it hard to relax. Telling someone, or writing the worry down before bed, can help your mind rest.
asks: Why do I worry at night?

faq.q: Does talking about a worry help?
faq.a: Yes. Saying a worry out loud makes it feel smaller, and the person you tell may help you make a plan. You do not have to carry it alone.
asks: Should I tell someone my worries?

faq.a: Yes, everyone worries sometimes, children and grown-ups too. A small worry can even help you get ready, like practising before a test.

faq.q: What if my worries feel too big?
faq.a: If worries are with you most of the time or stop you doing things, tell a grown-up you trust, a school counsellor or a doctor. Worries can be helped, and you are not alone.
asks: My worries will not go away

facts: In a 2019 study at Penn State University, about 91 percent of the worries people wrote down did not come true.
Worry is mostly about things that might happen in the future, while fear is usually about a danger right now.
